format.label: A memo to a CMO
format.instruction: Write it as a short internal memo to a chief marketing officer. Plain language, no jargon they would have to look up. Around 120 words.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Memo: Measurement at the budget level, not the ad level

I'd stop trying to see inside Performance Max. We won't. Instead treat each platform as one dial and measure the dial.

Start: an always-on experiment calendar, not one-off tests. Staggered geo on/off and budget step-changes running continuously, so we're always generating causal reads instead of waiting weeks for one. Small markets, cheap, repeated.

Those reads become the priors that make a mix model usable. Model alone, I don't trust; model plus a steady drip of experiments, I partly do.

Steering happens through inputs we still control: budget, feeds, exclusions, creative.

Expect: noisy early reads, six months before it's decision-grade, and platform changes we'll catch late. I'd rather be roughly right quarterly than precisely wrong daily.
answers.first_move: Pick two markets and start running continuous on/off budget tests in one channel, this month.
answers.hardest_part: The platforms change how they buy while we're measuring, so the thing we measured isn't quite the thing still running.

answers.label: ChatGPT
answers.approach:
To: CMO
Subject: Measuring what ads caused

I would not start by building a “better” attribution model. Without independent observations, added sophistication creates false certainty. I would narrow the goal from assigning credit to every conversion to estimating whether the next budget change will create incremental profit.

We should establish first-party outcome data, then run a permanent testing program: small rotating holdouts where feasible, matched-market tests for major changes, and deliberately staggered budget shifts. A time-varying model would combine those results with spend and sales data, but experiments would anchor it rather than merely “calibrate” it. We would judge the system by prospective predictions and publish ranges, disagreements, and failed tests.

This will not recover hidden placement-level truth. It should produce defensible budget guardrails and expose when evidence is too weak to steer.
answers.first_move: Define the specific budget decisions the measurement system must support.
answers.hardest_part: The hardest part is obtaining enough independent variation when platforms control delivery and most businesses cannot afford large holdouts.

answers.label: Gemini
answers.approach: We need to stop pretending another dashboard or vendor model will reveal which ad drove which sale. The platforms designed these black boxes specifically so we cannot see inside, and statistical models built on shifting algorithms produce comfortable fiction. My recommendation is to stop chasing continuous attribution. Instead, we should measure baseline business performance with intentional, periodic dark periods—turning channels completely off in selected regions—and accept that we can only measure total portfolio lift, not granular credit. Between tests, we steer spend by watching top-line customer acquisition costs against bank-account revenue, not platform dashboards. It limits how fast we react, but guessing based on distorted numbers is worse than moving slower with real truth.
answers.first_move: Run a clean, temporary blackout test on one major platform in a contained market to establish what happens to actual company revenue when that spend drops to zero.
answers.hardest_part: The ad algorithms constantly change how they find people while you test them, meaning the system you are trying to measure never sits still long enough to observe.

format.label: Three moves
format.instruction: Give exactly three moves, in order. One sentence each, then one sentence on what makes that move hard. Nothing else.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Move 1: Make forced variation a permanent line item — carve out 5-10% of budget as a standing perturbation fund that continuously jitters spend across geos, flights and channels on a randomized schedule, so causal reads accumulate as a time series of small shocks instead of being commissioned as six-week projects nobody has power for. What makes it hard: it requires finance and the CMO to accept a permanent, visible efficiency tax whose payoff is an error bar rather than revenue, and most orgs will quietly kill it the first bad quarter.

Move 2: Stop asking the model for channel truth and ask it only for the marginal return of the next dollar at current spend, feeding the perturbation results in as tight priors and reporting output as a decision (shift / hold / cut) with an explicit confidence threshold below which you don't act — I think the industry's insistence on channel-level ROI attribution is the actual error, because that number is unidentifiable at most budgets and you never needed it to make the allocation decision. What makes it hard: executives want a scoreboard, and "the credible interval says do nothing" is a politically unsurvivable answer even when it's correct.

Move 3: Treat platform behavior change as an observable event rather than model noise — monitor CPM distributions, delivery mix, conversion lag curves and auction-win proxies for change points, and use detected regime shifts to reset model windows and re-trigger perturbation rather than pretending the coefficient from four months ago still holds. What makes it hard: you're inferring a regime change from downstream symptoms that look identical to seasonality or a competitor's budget move, so you'll reset on false positives and bleed the statistical power you just spent money buying.
answers.first_move: Ring-fence a small, permanent slice of budget for randomized spend variation and start running it this quarter.
answers.hardest_part: The counterfactual you need is withheld by design, so no amount of cleverness recovers it — you can only buy it back with deliberately wasted spend, and the organization has to agree to keep paying for uncertainty it would rather not see.

answers.label: ChatGPT
answers.approach:
Move 1: Define decision-specific causal estimands—such as the incremental value of the next dollar by channel and week—and build an independent outcome ledger rather than trying to reconstruct the platforms’ missing user-level truth. What makes this hard is that inconsistent identities, conversion definitions, and exposure blind spots can leave even a precise estimand only partially identifiable.
Move 2: Create a continuous portfolio of small randomized perturbations—budget pulses, audience exclusions, switchbacks, matched geographies, and platform lift tests—and pool their evidence instead of waiting for occasional definitive holdouts. What makes this hard is that optimizer adaptation, cross-channel interference, limited power, and platform restrictions can invalidate the randomization or change the treatment while it is being measured.
Move 3: Use those experiments as time-varying anchors for an ensemble of dynamic causal models, report bounds and disagreement rather than one canonical attribution answer, and validate models by preregistering predictions for future withheld experiments. What makes this hard is that sparse experimental anchors and continuous platform drift may prevent tight estimates, so the system may support robust budget decisions without ever producing stable channel-level truth.
answers.first_move: First, decide exactly which budget decision must be measured and create an independent record of spend and business outcomes.
answers.hardest_part: The hardest part is separating genuine incremental demand from an adaptive platform’s targeting and optimization when the platform withholds the data needed for direct auditing.

answers.label: Gemini
answers.approach: 1. Deliberately inject programmed spend shocks into platform budgets rather than letting automated bidding algorithms operate smoothly. This is hard because media teams and leadership resist jeopardizing short-term revenue and resetting algorithmic learning states just to manufacture statistical variance. 2. Anchor all causal measurement strictly to downstream, bank-settled transaction ledgers rather than platform-reported conversion pixels. This is hard because conversion lag completely decouples financial truth from the rapid, intraday bidding loops automated platforms actually run on. 3. Abandon the search for a single, consensus ROI metric and replace it with heuristic decision thresholds that only reallocate capital when net margin shifts are unmistakable. This is hard because leadership routinely demands fictional precision to justify marketing budgets, making honest bounds of uncertainty culturally unacceptable.
answers.first_move: Deliberately inject sharp spend shocks into ad budgets to force observable variance.
answers.hardest_part: Ad platforms continuously alter their internal auction and targeting logic, constantly breaking the historical baselines that causal inference depends on.

format.label: Pseudocode
format.instruction: Express the approach as short annotated pseudocode. The comments should carry the reasoning; the code should carry the structure. Around 15 lines.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
```
# Premise I'd start from: the black box will never be auditable. Stop trying to decompose it.
# Measure only what you can steer; the estimand is the response of a *policy*, not of an ad.

levers = [budget, tCPA/tROAS, geo on/off, creative pool, audience signal]   # steerable == identifiable; ignore the rest
spine  = first_party_outcome                                               # one trusted outcome, never platform conversions,
                                                                           # frozen even when it's the wrong KPI - drift kills comparability

loop forever:                                      # continuous jitter, not a 6-week "test" you have to get budget approved for
  cells = switchback(geo x week, stratified by baseline volume, buffer borders)  # borders leak; buffer or accept bias
  apply(jitter(lever, +/-15%))                     # small enough to be free in expectation, permanent so power accrues over time
  theta_t = bayes_update(theta_{t-1}, spine(cells),
                         prior = partial_pool(peer_accounts, vertical, channel))  # pooling across accounts is the only honest
                                                                                  # fix for underpowered budgets. Requires a
                                                                                  # consortium - this is a business problem, not a math one
  if changepoint(theta_t): widen_intervals(); flag("platform re-optimized")  # don't model non-stationarity away; detect it.
                                                                             # the jitter doubles as the stationarity monitor
  mmm.calibrate(theta_t)                           # MMM demoted: interpolator between experiments, not the estimator
  publish(predicted_lift[t+1])                     # pre-register before the read, or you're fitting

score = calibration(predicted_lift, realized_lift) # the missing benchmark is forecast accuracy on unseen periods, not in-sample fit
trust(mmm) if score in band else trust(theta_t) only  # vendor disagreement resolves on prediction, nothing else
```
Where I disagree with the obvious answer: the standard prescription is "MMM calibrated with geo lifts." That's directionally right and operationally dead, because it treats calibration as an event. The fix isn't a better model, it's making experimentation so cheap it never stops - and accepting that the output is a steering signal with wide intervals, not an attribution number.

What I expect to run into: (1) the perturbation is itself an input to the optimizer, so you're measuring a system adapting to you - the dose-response curve you recover may not exist off-experiment; (2) pacing means a down-week gets repaid in the up-week, contaminating switchbacks; (3) cross-channel cannibalization makes single-lever jitter non-separable; (4) the pooled prior is where the real power comes from, and nobody wants to share.
answers.first_move: Freeze a single first-party outcome metric and start jittering budget by ±15% across randomized geo-weeks on the biggest channel, before building any model.
answers.hardest_part: You are perturbing a learning system that responds to your perturbation, so there may be no stable dose-response curve underneath to recover.

format.label: A checklist
format.instruction: Give a checklist someone could actually run next quarter. Each item concrete enough to be marked done or not done. Six items at most.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Position first: stop trying to audit the black box. You will not get placement/query-level truth back, and the effort spent litigating platform-reported conversions is the single biggest waste of measurement headcount I see. The only things you still control are the budget dial, the objective you feed the system, and the structural boundaries you draw around it. Measure those. Everything below follows from that.

1. **Decision ledger + MDE reality check (weeks 1-3).** Write down every decision measurement is supposed to inform this year, the dollar swing attached to it, and the effect size that would actually change the call. Then compute the minimum detectable effect of your current test capability at current budget. Done = a one-page table where each decision is marked "detectable" or "not detectable." Expect half to be undetectable; kill the measurement work attached to those and make those calls on judgment, openly. Most teams run tests that mathematically cannot see their own effect and then argue about the result.

2. **Always-on experiment program, not a test calendar (launch by week 6).** The fix for underpowered geo tests is not bigger geos, it's continuous accrual: rotating geo holdouts, staggered/switchback rollouts, sequential (always-valid) analysis so you can stop early, and larger, cruder levers — full-platform pauses and 40%+ spend steps rather than 10% nudges nobody can see. Done = N tests launched per quarter with pre-registered power calculations, raw geo-day panel retained in your warehouse, results in a shared repository. Target 6-10 reads a year, not two. The first two will be a mess; run them anyway.

3. **Platform change journal (week 4, then permanent).** Pull campaign change history via API nightly plus a manual log of every bid-strategy, feed, value-rule and asset-group change, timestamped. This is cheap, almost nobody does it, and it is the only defense against non-stationarity: you model epochs between changes, not a stable "channel coefficient." Done = automated daily ingest, with changes joinable to the spend panel.

4. **Change what it maximizes instead of auditing what it reports (quarter-long).** Push a profit- or new-customer-weighted value signal back via offline conversion import, and structurally fence brand/existing-customer demand out of the automated campaigns so the black box isn't being paid to harvest what you already own. This is the highest-leverage item on the list: self-attribution bias matters far less when the objective is one you'd actually sign off on. Done = X% of automated spend bidding to a margin- or NC-weighted value, with a documented lag/match-rate on the feedback loop.

5. **Bake-off on held-out experiments, pre-registered (quarter 2).** Do not buy or build an MMM until you have a calibration bank. Then make every candidate (Meridian, Robyn, vendor, internal) predict the results of experiments it never saw, scored on a rule written before the results are known. Done = a leaderboard with out-of-sample error per model. Treat MMM as interpolation between experiments and a budget-planning prior, not as a measurement instrument — if a vendor can't pass this, their credible intervals are decoration.

6. **Reconciliation policy and a learning budget line (by quarter end).** One written page: platform numbers steer in-flight only, experiments are truth, MMM fills the gaps, and here is what happens when they disagree. Attach a standing 3-7% of spend as the cost of learning, approved by finance as a line item rather than scavenged per test. Done = signed by the person who owns the budget, plus a quarterly "what we still don't know" memo with intervals published rather than hidden.

What I'd expect to run into: the feedback-loop item (4) breaks on identity match rates and conversion lag before it breaks on anything clever; your first three experiments will produce intervals wide enough to be unsatisfying and someone senior will use that to dismiss the program; and the platforms will change optimization behavior mid-test at least once, which is why item 3 exists. Realistically you get a usable read on one or two big questions in nine months, not a measurement system in a quarter.
answers.first_move: Write down the decisions measurement is supposed to drive and check whether any test you can afford could actually detect an effect big enough to change them.
answers.hardest_part: Incrementality is a property of a system that changes faster than you can measure it, so by the time a read is trustworthy the thing you measured no longer exists.

answers.label: ChatGPT
answers.approach:
- [ ] **Define two decisions and their estimands.** Pick no more than two material questions—such as “move 15% from PMax to paid social?”—and specify population, horizon, counterfactual, and acceptable uncertainty. Treat each platform’s AI buyer as a black-box treatment; do not promise placement-, query-, or creative-level causality that the available data cannot identify.
- [ ] **Build an auditable measurement spine.** Reconcile first-party outcomes, spend, exposure aggregates, consent coverage, conversion lag, promotions, pricing, inventory, and platform-reported conversions by day and market. Version every extract and maintain a dated log of campaign, bidding, attribution, and platform-product changes; publish the unexplained reconciliation gaps.
- [ ] **Power interventions before running them.** Using historical variance and realistic effect sizes, simulate user holdouts, matched-geo tests, geo-time switchbacks, and randomized budget pulses. Mark designs infeasible when expected precision cannot support the chosen decision rather than running underpowered tests and calling null results “no incrementality.”
- [ ] **Run a small intervention portfolio.** Execute at least one platform-randomized holdout where available and one independently controlled geo/time budget perturbation, with preregistered assignment, guardrails, contamination checks, lag windows, and stopping rules. Use multiple treatment intensities if feasible to learn marginal response rather than only on/off lift.
- [ ] **Fit competing models and force prospective validation.** Compare a time-varying state-space MMM, a simpler causal time-series model, and experiment-only estimates. Calibrate only with completed interventions, freeze each model before the next intervention, and score its prediction of direction, magnitude, and uncertainty coverage; model disagreement remains an output, not something to average away.
- [ ] **Ship a decision report with explicit failure rules.** For each budget decision, report an effect range, probability the move is beneficial, sensitivity to attribution and lag assumptions, transportability limits, and the result each method produced. Precommit to “no recommendation” when methods conflict materially or intervals cross the decision threshold, and use the next quarter’s intervention to target the largest unresolved disagreement.
answers.first_move: Choose one real budget decision and write down exactly what causal effect must be known to make it.
answers.hardest_part: Platform optimization creates interference and changes the treatment during measurement, so weak external interventions may never identify a stable effect that transports to the next budget decision.
